title: How does static behave in inheritance (static variable hiding, static method hiding vs overriding, static block execution order, and why super cannot call a static method)?
shortTitle: How does static behave in inheritance?

s1_definition.profdef: Static members are associated with the class, not with instances, so they participate in inheritance by hiding rather than by overriding. A subclass static field with the same name hides the parent's static field, and the version used is determined at compile time by the reference type, not by the runtime object. Likewise a static method with the same signature in a subclass hides the parent's static method; it is not polymorphically overridden, so the method invoked is chosen by the declared type, not dynamic dispatch. Static initializer blocks run in the order of class loading, parent class before child class. The `super` keyword cannot invoke a static method because static methods are not instance-bound and have no dynamic dispatch, so there is nothing for `super` to resolve against an instance.
s1_definition.analogy: At the National Bank of India, imagine head office defines a standard fee procedure and the regional office defines its own procedure with the same name. With instance methods this is like overriding, where the actual branch that serves you decides which procedure runs. But static methods are like notices pinned to a specific office's wall: which notice you read depends on which office's address you looked up, not on which customer walked in. If you address the lookup to head office you get head office's notice even if the regional office pinned a newer one. And you cannot say "use my parent office's static notice through super", because static notices belong to offices, not to a specific customer instance.
s1_definition.oneliner: Static members are hidden, not overridden — resolution is by compile-time reference type, parent static blocks run before child, and super cannot call static methods.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Static members are associated with the class, not with instances, so they participate in inheritance by hiding rather than by overriding. A subclass static field with the same name hides the parent's static field, and the version used is determined at compile time by the reference type, not by the runtime object. Likewise a static method with the same signature in a subclass hides the parent's static method; it is not polymorphically overridden, so the method invoked is chosen by the declared type, not dynamic dispatch. Static initializer blocks run in the order of class loading, parent class before child class. The `super` keyword cannot invoke a static method because static methods are not instance-bound and have no dynamic dispatch, so there is nothing for `super` to resolve against an instance.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** At the National Bank of India, imagine head office defines a standard fee procedure and the regional office defines its own procedure with the same name. With instance methods this is like overriding, where the actual branch that serves you decides which procedure runs. But static methods are like notices pinned to a specific office's wall: which notice you read depends on which office's address you looked up, not on which customer walked in. If you address the lookup to head office you get head office's notice even if the regional office pinned a newer one. And you cannot say "use my parent office's static notice through super", because static notices belong to offices, not to a specific customer instance.

**One line to remember:** Static members are hidden, not overridden — resolution is by compile-time reference type, parent static blocks run before child, and super cannot call static methods.

sections.s2_technical:
Static variable hiding: if a parent class declares a static field and the child declares a static field with the same name, the child's field hides the parent's. Which one you access depends on the compile-time type of the reference. Through a `Parent` reference you see the parent's field even if the object is actually a `Child`. This is because static access is resolved at compile time by type, with no runtime polymorphism.

Static method hiding versus overriding: instance methods are overridden and use dynamic dispatch, so the runtime type of the object decides which method runs. Static methods are not overridden; a same-signature static method in the child hides the parent's. The method that runs is decided by the declared type at compile time. Marking a hidden static method with `@Override` is a compile error, which is the compiler telling you static methods cannot be overridden.

Static block execution order: when a class is initialized, its superclass is initialized first. So static initializer blocks run parent first, then child, and within a class they run in textual order along with static field initializers. This ordering happens once, at class loading, and before any instance of the class is created.

Why super cannot call a static method: `super` is a mechanism for an instance to reach its parent's instance behavior through the object. Static methods belong to the class and have no `this` and no dynamic dispatch, so there is no instance context for `super` to use. If you want the parent's static method, you simply name it through the parent class, like `Parent.staticMethod()`. A senior nuance is that calling a static method through an instance reference, such as `obj.staticMethod()`, is legal but misleading, because the method resolves by the reference's declared type, not the object; good code always calls static methods through the class name to avoid this confusion. Another nuance is that these hiding rules are a frequent source of subtle bugs, so in banking code we avoid same-named static members across a hierarchy entirely.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank has a base Account type with a static category label and a subclass SavingsAccount with its own static category label of the same name. A report accidentally showed the wrong category because it accessed the field through a base reference. This is exactly static variable hiding resolved by reference type.

Problem 2 — Both classes define a static `accountType` method with the same signature. A developer expected polymorphism but got the base version through a base reference. This is exactly static method hiding, not overriding.

Problem 3 — The team must understand that static blocks ran parent first then child during class loading, and that attempting to call the parent static method via super failed to compile. This is exactly static block ordering and the super restriction.

The code has an `Account` base and `SavingsAccount` subclass each with a static field, a static method, and a static block, and a `StaticInheritanceDemo` main class that demonstrates hiding through different reference types.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: a SavingsAccount object viewed through both a SavingsAccount reference and a base Account reference.

Step 1: The program first references SavingsAccount, which forces class loading. The JVM initializes the superclass Account first, so Account's static block runs and logs that the parent loaded first.

Step 2: Then SavingsAccount's static block runs, logging that the child loaded second. This proves static blocks run parent before child, once, at class loading.

Step 3: The static field CATEGORY is accessed. Through the Account class it reports GENERIC, and through SavingsAccount it reports SAVINGS. The child's field hides the parent's, and which one is seen depends purely on the compile-time type used to access it.

Step 4: The same object assigned to a base reference still sees the base category when accessed through that reference, confirming there is no runtime polymorphism for static fields.

Step 5: The static method accountType is called. Through Account it returns BASE, and through SavingsAccount it returns SAVINGS. This is hiding by declared type, not overriding by runtime object.

Step 6: Attempting to call the parent's static method through super would not compile, because static methods have no instance dispatch for super to resolve. The correct way to reach it is to name the parent class directly.

```text
INFO: Static block: Account loaded (parent first)
INFO: Static block: SavingsAccount loaded (child second)
INFO: asBase.CATEGORY   = GENERIC
INFO: SavingsAccount.CATEGORY = SAVINGS
INFO: Account.accountType()        = BASE
INFO: SavingsAccount.accountType()  = SAVINGS
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```text
  reference SavingsAccount → trigger class loading
    │
    ▼ initialize superclass FIRST
  Account static {}  → "parent first"
    │
    ▼ then child
  SavingsAccount static {} → "child second"

  Access CATEGORY (static field):
    via Account type        → GENERIC   (parent field)
    via SavingsAccount type → SAVINGS   (child field HIDES parent)
    (same object, resolved by REFERENCE TYPE, not runtime object)

  Call accountType() (static method):
    Account.accountType()        → BASE
    SavingsAccount.accountType() → SAVINGS  (HIDES, not overrides)

  super.accountType() compile error (no static dispatch)
```
sections.s5c_hld:
```text
  ═══ HLD — Reporting Service over Account Hierarchy ═══

  ┌────────────┐  REST   ┌──────────────────┐
  │ Reporting  │───────→ │ CategoryResolver │
  │ UI         │         │ (reads static    │
  └────────────┘         │  category labels)│
                         └────────┬─────────┘
                                  │ CAUTION
                                  ▼
                 ┌───────────────────────────────┐

                 │ SavingsAccount (static CATEGORY)│
                 └───────────────────────────────┘
   Risk: accessing via base reference returns parent label.

```
sections.s5d_lld:
```text
  ═══ LLD — Hiding vs Overriding ═══

  ┌───────────────────────────────┐
  │           Account             │
  │ static CATEGORY = "GENERIC"   │
  │ static accountType(): "BASE"  │
  │ static {} "parent first"      │
  └───────────────┬───────────────┘
                  │ extends
                  ▼
  ┌───────────────────────────────┐
  │        SavingsAccount         │
  │ static CATEGORY = "SAVINGS"   │  ◀ HIDES parent field
  │ static accountType():"SAVINGS"│  ◀ HIDES parent method
  │ static {} "child second"      │
  └───────────────────────────────┘

  Rules table (as rules):
   static field  → HIDDEN, resolved by compile-time reference type
   static method → HIDDEN (not overridden), resolved by declared type
   instance method → OVERRIDDEN, resolved by runtime object (dynamic)
   static blocks → parent runs before child, once, at class load
   super.staticMethod() → ILLEGAL (no instance dispatch)
   @Override on static → COMPILE ERROR
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
Static members participate in inheritance by hiding, not by overriding, and understanding that distinction is the heart of this question. Because static members belong to the class and not to instances, there is no dynamic dispatch for them.

For static variables, if a subclass declares a static field with the same name as the parent, the subclass field hides the parent field. Which one I actually get is decided at compile time by the type of the reference, not by the runtime object. So the same object viewed through a base-class reference sees the base field, while through a subclass reference it sees the subclass field. There is no polymorphism.

For static methods, the same rule applies. A same-signature static method in the subclass hides the parent's static method rather than overriding it. The method that runs is chosen by the declared type at compile time, not by the runtime object. In fact, if I put an Override annotation on a hidden static method, the compiler rejects it, which is the language telling me static methods cannot be overridden.

Static initializer blocks run in class-loading order, which means the parent class is initialized before the child, so the parent's static block runs first, then the child's, and this happens exactly once, before any instance exists. And super cannot call a static method, because super is a mechanism for an instance to reach its parent's instance behavior, while static methods have no instance and no dynamic dispatch; if I want the parent's static method I just name it through the parent class directly.

In practice, in our banking code, I treat these hiding rules as a warning sign rather than a feature. They are a well-known source of subtle bugs, like a report showing the wrong account category because it read a static field through a base reference. So I avoid same-named static members across a class hierarchy entirely, and when I need type-specific behavior I use instance methods with proper overriding, or an enum, so that resolution follows the actual object and not the declared reference type.

---

keyPoints: Static fields: inherited but shared — child sees parent static
Static methods: inherited but hidden (not overridden)
Method hiding: child can declare same-signature static method
Resolution: static dispatch by reference type, not actual object type
